title: Authentication vs Authorization
subtitle: Identity vs rights: factors & MFA, biometrics, Kerberos/RADIUS/LDAP/OAuth, SSO & access-control models

readingSections.title: The Core Distinction: Who vs What
readingSections.quickSummary: Authentication verifies IDENTITY (who are you?); authorization grants RIGHTS (what may you do?). AuthN always precedes AuthZ.
content: Authentication (AuthN) verifies a user's identity by comparing presented credentials against an authorised-user database - username/password, cards, retina scans, voice recognition, fingerprints. It establishes and confirms WHO the person or system is, and has no bearing on which tasks or files that identity may touch.

Authorization (AuthZ) determines access rights: the system (typically a server administrator in multi-user systems) defines which users reach which directories, at which hours, with how much storage. It answers WHAT the verified identity may do, usually immediately after authentication.

The pairing rules from the syllabus: authentication is used when a SERVER wants to know exactly who is accessing it, and when a CLIENT wants proof the server is genuine (mutual authentication). Authorization is the process by which a server assesses whether a client has PERMISSION to use a resource. Some systems have no authorization at all - any requester gets the resource; most public web pages require neither.

subsections.title: The exam mapping (memorise verbatim)
subsections.content:
'Process of verifying a user's identity' -> AUTHENTICATION.
'Process of assessing whether a client has permission to use a resource' -> AUTHORIZATION.
'Credentials compared to a database of authorised users' -> AUTHENTICATION.
'Defines directories, hours of access, storage space' -> AUTHORIZATION.

quickRevision: AuthN = who you are (identity). AuthZ = what you may do (rights).
AuthN first, AuthZ second - always in that order.
AuthN methods: passwords, cards, retina, voice, fingerprints.
AuthZ may require additional authentication in some cases; some systems have none.
tricks: AuthenticatioN contains 'identification' - identity is authentication, every time.
Password in the stem -> authentication. Permission/privilege/rights in the stem -> authorization.
Biometrics (fingerprint, retina, voice) are ALWAYS authentication - never authorization.
patterns: 'Server wants to know exactly WHO is accessing' -> authentication.
'Server assesses whether the client has permission' -> authorization.

pyqPatterns.question: Difference between authorization and authentication - which statement is true?
pyqPatterns.approach: Any option swapping the two is wrong: identity = AuthN, rights = AuthZ.

readingSections.companyNote: This is a named official AXIS topic - expect at least one direct AuthN-vs-AuthZ question per slot.

readingSections.title: Authentication Factors & MFA
readingSections.quickSummary: Three factor families: know (password/PIN), have (card/OTP phone), are (fingerprint/face/voice). MFA mixes families; two passwords is still single-factor.
content: Knowledge factor - something you KNOW: passwords, PINs, security questions. Cheapest, weakest (guessable, phishable, reusable).
Possession factor - something you HAVE: smart cards, hardware tokens, OTP apps, phone push-approval. Stronger: theft is noticeable.

Inherence factor - something you ARE: fingerprints, retina/iris scans, voice recognition, facial geometry - the biometrics the syllabus lists. Cannot be forgotten or shared, but can't be rotated after compromise.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA/2FA) requires factors from DIFFERENT families: password + OTP app, card + PIN, fingerprint + phone. Two different passwords = still single-factor. Location/behaviour ('somewhere you are', 'something you do') appear as extended factors in some textbooks.

subsections.title: Biometric accuracy vocabulary
subsections.content:
FAR (False Acceptance Rate) - impostors wrongly accepted.
FRR (False Rejection Rate) - genuine users wrongly rejected.
CER/EER (Crossover Error Rate) - where FAR = FRR; LOWER CER = better device.
Retention/registration - enrolling the template; templates should be stored as irreversible mathematical representations.

quickRevision: Know / Have / Are - the three factor families.
tricks: OTP + password = MFA; password + PIN = single factor - the classic trap pair.
'Something you ARE' options are always authentication methods.
Biometric accuracy question: pick the LOWEST CER/EER.
patterns: 'Which is a possession factor?' - smart card/OTP token.
'Which improves security by combining factors?' - MFA.

pyqPatterns.question: Cards, retina scans, voice recognition and fingerprints are listed as:
pyqPatterns.approach: Authentication methods (the syllabus lists them verbatim alongside username/password).

readingSections.companyNote: Factor-family classification is a reliable one-mark question - the password+PIN trap appears everywhere.

readingSections.title: Enterprise AuthN/AuthZ Protocols
readingSections.quickSummary: Kerberos = ticket-based domain auth; RADIUS/TACACS+ = network access AAA; LDAP = directory queries; SAML/OAuth/OpenID = web SSO; 802.1X = port-based access.
content: KERBEROS is the domain authentication protocol (Windows Active Directory's core): a trusted third party (Key Distribution Center) issues TICKETS instead of sending passwords over the network. The client proves identity to the TGT-issuing service, then presents service tickets to individual servers - mutual authentication with timestamps defeating replays.

RADIUS (UDP 1812/1645) and TACACS+ (TCP 49) are AAA protocols - Authentication, Authorization, Accounting - for network access: VPN concentrators, Wi-Fi, switches. RADIUS encrypts only the password field; TACACS+ encrypts the entire payload and separates the three As - Cisco's favourite exam contrast.
LDAP (port 389/636) queries DIRECTORY services - the database of users/groups that authorization decisions consult. Active Directory is LDAP + Kerberos + DNS together.

Web SSO protocols: SAML (XML assertions, enterprise SSO), OAuth 2.0 (DELEGATED AUTHORIZATION - 'login with X' granting scoped access without sharing passwords), OpenID Connect (authentication layer on OAuth). Single Sign-On = authenticate once, access many systems.
802.1X = port-based network access control: a device must authenticate (usually via RADIUS) before the switch port passes traffic.

subsections.title: AAA decoded
subsections.content:
Authentication - who are you? (credentials verified)
Authorization - what may you do? (rights applied)
Accounting - what did you do? (logging/auditing: session time, data, commands)

quickRevision: Kerberos = tickets, no passwords on the wire, Active Directory.
RADIUS (UDP, password-only encryption) vs TACACS+ (TCP, full encryption, separated AAA).
OAuth = delegated authorization; OpenID = authentication; SAML = enterprise SSO assertions.
tricks: 'AAA' in the stem -> RADIUS or TACACS+; 'Cisco' or 'full payload encryption' tips it to TACACS+.
'Authenticate once, use many apps' -> SSO (SAML in enterprises).
patterns: 'Which AAA protocol encrypts the entire session?' - TACACS+.

pyqPatterns.question: Which protocol provides SSO in Windows domains?
pyqPatterns.approach: Kerberos - the Active Directory authentication core.

readingSections.companyNote: Protocol-identification questions (Kerberos/RADIUS/LDAP/OAuth) appear in the broader technical pool and interviews.

readingSections.title: Access Control Models
readingSections.quickSummary: DAC = owner decides; MAC = labels/levels (military); RBAC = roles define rights; ABAC = attribute rules. Plus least privilege & separation of duties.
content: DAC (Discretionary Access Control): the resource OWNER decides who gets access (file permissions you set). Flexible, but owners can misconfigure and permissions propagate (Trojan horses ride DAC).

MAC (Mandatory Access Control): the SYSTEM enforces access by SECURITY LABELS and clearance levels - military/classified models (Top Secret/Secret/Confidential). Owners cannot override; no read-up, no write-down (Bell-LaPadula).

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): rights attach to ROLES (teller, manager, admin); users are assigned roles. Enterprise standard - matches org charts, simplifies administration, enables separation of duties.
ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): policies evaluate ATTRIBUTES (user department, time, device health, location) - the finest-grained, powering zero-trust policies.
Governing principles: LEAST PRIVILEGE (minimum rights needed), SEPARATION OF DUTIES (no single person controls a whole sensitive process - the initiator cannot also approve).

subsections.title: Model identification phrases
subsections.content:
'Owner decides' -> DAC.
'Labels and clearance levels, system-enforced' -> MAC.
'Rights assigned via job functions/roles' -> RBAC.
'Policies on attributes like time/device/location' -> ABAC.

quickRevision: DAC owner-decides; MAC label-enforced; RBAC role-driven; ABAC attribute-rules.
Least privilege + separation of duties govern all models.
Military/classified -> MAC. Corporate org chart -> RBAC.
tricks: 'Cannot override the system's labels' -> MAC (the owner is powerless - the giveaway).
'Teller role can approve accounts but not audit them' -> RBAC + separation of duties.

pyqPatterns.question: Which access model uses security labels and clearances?

readingSections.companyNote: Access-model identification appears in security buckets and interviews alike - four definitions, four marks.

formulas.title: Three Factor Families

formula.text: Knowledge (password/PIN), possession (card/OTP), inherence (biometrics). MFA mixes families.

explanation: Knowledge: passwords, PINs, security questions.
Possession: smart cards, OTP tokens, phones.
Inherence: fingerprint, retina, voice, face.
MFA = factors from DIFFERENT families; two passwords stays single-factor.
Extended factors: somewhere you are (location), something you do (behaviour).

example.prompt: Password plus fingerprint login - what is this?

formulas.title: AAA & Auth Protocol Map

formula.text: Match each protocol to its single signature purpose.

explanation: Kerberos: ticket-based domain auth (Active Directory); no passwords on the wire; mutual auth.
RADIUS: UDP, AAA for network access, encrypts password field only.
TACACS+: TCP, encrypts full payload, separates AAA (Cisco).
LDAP 389/636: directory queries (users/groups).
SAML: enterprise SSO assertions; OAuth 2.0: delegated authorization; OpenID Connect: authN layer.
802.1X: port-based access control before traffic passes.

example.prompt: Which protocol issues tickets instead of transmitting passwords?

formulas.commonMistake: OAuth as authentication - OAuth authorizes; OpenID authenticates.

formulas.title: Biometric Accuracy Metrics

formula.text: FAR = impostors accepted; FRR = genuine users rejected; the crossover rate ranks devices.

explanation: FAR (False Acceptance): security risk - impostors pass.
FRR (False Rejection): usability pain - genuine users bounce.
CER/EER: the sensitivity point where FAR = FRR; the LOWER the CER, the better the device.
Templates stored as irreversible mathematical representations.

example.answer: The device with the lowest CER/EER

formulas.memoryTip: Accept-false = FAR risk; Reject-false = FRR pain.
formulas.commonMistake: Choosing the HIGHEST CER - lower is always better.

formulas.title: Access Control Models

formula.text: Four models: owner-decided, label-enforced, role-driven, attribute-rule-based.

explanation: DAC: resource owners grant access (file permissions); flexible, error-prone.
MAC: system-enforced labels/clearances (military); no owner override.
RBAC: rights attach to roles; enterprise standard.
ABAC: policies on attributes (dept, time, device, location) - zero-trust grade granularity.
Principles: least privilege, separation of duties.

example.prompt: Rights assigned through job functions like 'teller' or 'auditor'.

formulas.commonMistake: Calling label-based access 'RBAC' - labels/clearances are MAC.

formulas.title: SSO & Delegation Flow

formula.text: Single Sign-On exchanges tokens/assertions instead of re-prompting credentials.

explanation: SSO: authenticate once against an IdP (identity provider); apps trust its assertions.
SAML: XML assertions; enterprise web SSO.
OAuth 2.0: resource owner grants SCOPED access to a third party WITHOUT sharing the password.
OpenID Connect: OAuth + authentication layer (who logged in).
Benefit/risk: one strong login, but one high-value target.

example.prompt: 'Login with Google' on a third-party site.
steps: Delegated, scoped access without password sharing.

formulas.memoryTip: One login, many doors; OAuth delegates, OpenID identifies.
formulas.commonMistake: 'Login with X' called SAML - consumer flows are OAuth/OIDC; SAML is enterprise SSO.

mcqs.q: Authentication verifies:
exp: Identity verification against an authorised-user database.

mcqs.q: Authorization determines:
exp: Rights: directories, hours, storage - decided after identity is known.

mcqs.q: Which is an authentication method per the AXIS syllabus?
exp: Cards, retina scans, voice recognition and fingerprints are syllabus-listed authentication methods.

mcqs.q: Which process runs FIRST?
exp: Identity before rights - always.

mcqs.q: A password is which factor?
exp: Something you KNOW = knowledge factor.

mcqs.q: A fingerprint scan is which factor?
exp: Something you ARE - inherence (biometric).

mcqs.q: An OTP app on your phone is which factor?
exp: Something you HAVE - possession.

mcqs.q: Password + OTP approval is:
exp: Knowledge + possession = different families = MFA.

mcqs.q: Password + PIN together is:
exp: Same family (knowledge) - the classic MFA trap.

mcqs.q: Which protocol issues TICKETS instead of sending passwords over the network?
exp: Kerberos tickets via the Key Distribution Center - Active Directory's core.

mcqs.q: Kerberos is the authentication core of:
exp: AD = LDAP + Kerberos + DNS.

mcqs.q: AAA stands for:
exp: Who are you, what may you do, what did you do.

mcqs.q: LDAP is used to:
exp: The directory database authorization decisions consult (ports 389/636).

mcqs.q: 'Login with Google' on a third-party app is:
exp: Scoped access without password sharing = OAuth 2.0 (OpenID adds identity).

mcqs.q: 802.1X provides:
exp: Authenticate before the switch port passes traffic (usually via RADIUS).

mcqs.q: Which access model lets the resource OWNER decide permissions?
exp: Discretionary = owner's discretion (your file permissions).

mcqs.q: Which model uses security LABELS and CLEARANCES?
exp: Mandatory Access Control - military/classified, system-enforced.

mcqs.q: Rights attached to job functions like 'teller' describe:
exp: Role-Based Access Control - rights follow roles, not individuals.

mcqs.q: The principle of granting minimum needed rights is:
exp: Shrinks the blast radius of any compromise.

mcqs.q: RADIUS typically runs over:
exp: UDP 1812/1645 - encrypts only the password field.

mcqs.q: Which AAA protocol encrypts the ENTIRE payload and separates the three As?
exp: TACACS+ (TCP 49) - Cisco's contrast favourite.

mcqs.q: Biometric device accuracy is ranked by:
exp: CER/EER = the FAR=FRR point; lower is better.

mcqs.q: FAR (False Acceptance Rate) measures:
exp: FAR = the security risk; FRR = the usability pain.

mcqs.q: Single Sign-On means:
exp: IdP-issued tokens/assertions trusted across apps (SAML/OIDC).

mcqs.q: Which model enforces access by attributes like TIME and DEVICE HEALTH?
exp: Attribute-Based Access Control - zero-trust grade policies.

mcqs.q: Separation of duties means:
opts: No single person controls an entire sensitive process
exp: Initiator cannot also approve - fraud/failure containment.

mcqs.q: Which is TRUE about most public web pages?
opts: They require neither authentication nor authorization
exp: Public resources: no gate at all - the syllabus' own line.

mcqs.q: A server wanting to know exactly WHO is accessing uses:
exp: Identity verification = authentication (client-side proof too - mutual auth).

mcqs.q: Authorization may sometimes require:
exp: Syllabus: passwords necessary in some cases, not others.

mcqs.q: SAML is primarily used for:
exp: XML assertion-based SSO between identity and service providers.

mcqs.q: OpenID Connect adds to OAuth 2.0:
exp: OAuth authorizes; OIDC answers 'who logged in'.

mcqs.q: Kerberos defeats replay attacks using:
exp: Captured tickets expire quickly and carry time validation.

mcqs.q: Which model can an owner NOT override?
exp: Mandatory = system-enforced labels; owners have no discretion.

mcqs.q: Biometric templates should be stored as:
exp: You can rotate a password, never a fingerprint - store only irreversible templates.

mcqs.q: Which is an ACCOUNTING example?
opts: Logging session duration and data transferred
exp: Accounting = the 'what did you do' audit leg of AAA.

mcqs.q: Mutual authentication means:
opts: Both client and server prove identity
exp: Kerberos and certificate mutual TLS both provide it - the syllabus notes clients verifying servers too.

mcqs.q: Which factor is 'somewhere you are'?
exp: Geolocation appears as an extended/contextual factor.

mcqs.q: RBAC's main administrative benefit:
opts: Rights follow roles, simplifying management as people change jobs
exp: Change a user's role; all rights follow - no per-resource edits.

mcqs.q: Which is a POSSESSION factor example?
exp: Something you HAVE - cards, tokens, phones.

mcqs.q: Authorization without any authentication is:
opts: Possible in systems where any requester gets the resource
exp: Syllabus: in some circumstances there is no authorization - anyone requesting gets it; and some systems skip authz entirely.

mcqs.q: A published syllabus line says authentication 'has no bearing on' which files/tasks a user may access. This is emphasised because candidates confuse:
exp: The syllabus stresses identity-proofing grants NOTHING - rights are authorization's domain.

mcqs.q: Why does Kerberos avoid sending passwords over the network?
opts: Ticket-based exchange with time-limited encrypted tickets replaces password transmission
exp: Credentials prove identity once to the KDC; tickets (encrypted, timestamped) speak thereafter.

mcqs.q: A company wants network-device administration to log EVERY command separately with full-payload encryption. Choose:
exp: TACACS+ separates AAA and encrypts full payloads - command-by-command accounting included.

mcqs.q: An attacker steals a fingerprint template database. Why is this worse than a password leak?
opts: Biometrics cannot be rotated/changed after compromise
exp: You get ten fingers for life - template protection (irreversible storage) is critical.

mcqs.q: A zero-trust policy allows finance app access only from managed laptops 9-to-5. Which model?
exp: Device-health + time + department attributes = ABAC policy evaluation.

mcqs.q: OAuth's 'scoped access' means the third-party app:
opts: Receives limited rights (e.g., read-only calendar) without your password
exp: Delegated authorization: specific scopes, revocable, no credential sharing.

mcqs.q: Which sequence is a correct Kerberos exchange?
opts: Auth to KDC -> receive TGT -> request service ticket -> present to service
exp: KDC/AS issues TGT; TGS issues service tickets; services validate tickets - no passwords on the wire.

mcqs.q: Bell-LaPadula's 'no read up, no write down' belongs to which model?
exp: Clearance labels enforce confidentiality lattices - mandatory, not discretionary.

mcqs.q: An org requires that the person who INITIATES payments cannot APPROVE them. Which principle?
exp: SoD splits critical processes across roles - RBAC implements it.

mcqs.q: Why is 'password + security question' usually still single-factor?
opts: Both are knowledge factors answerable by the same attacker research
exp: Family matters, not count - security questions are knowledge, phishable like passwords.

mcqs.q: Which deployment gives SSO AND centralized authorization policy in a web estate?
opts: Identity Provider with SAML/OIDC + central policy (e.g., IdP groups mapped per app)
exp: Central IdP: one authentication, group-driven authorization pushed to apps.

mcqs.q: RADIUS vs TACACS+ classic contrast pair:
opts: RADIUS: UDP, merges AAA, hides password; TACACS+: TCP, separate AAA, full encryption
RADIUS: TCP, full encryption; TACACS+: UDP
exp: The canonical exam contrast - transport, payload scope, and AAA separation.

mcqs.q: A biometric door reads a severed finger as valid. Which metric failed the designers?
exp: Presentation/liveness detection defeats spoofing - pure FAR maths missed liveness.

mcqs.q: Which statement about OAuth scopes is TRUE?
opts: Scopes limit WHAT the app may do (e.g., read-only calendar) and are revocable
exp: Delegated authorization = narrow, revocable grants - never the full account.

mcqs.q: 802.1X with EAP-TLS authenticates:
opts: Both the user/device AND the network via certificates
exp: Certificate-based mutual auth before the port opens - the enterprise NAC standard.

mcqs.q: Which access model would a military classified system with Top Secret/Secret labels use?
exp: Clearance labels enforced by the system = mandatory access control.

mcqs.q: A helpdesk can reset passwords but not view salaries; HR views salaries but cannot reset passwords. This is:
exp: Role-scoped rights + split sensitive processes = textbook RBAC/SoD.

mcqs.q: Why do enterprises prefer central IdP SSO over per-app accounts?
opts: One hardened authentication point, instant deprovisioning, consistent MFA policy
exp: Central authN/authZ: one place to enforce MFA and cut access when people leave.

mcqs.q: Which option correctly pairs protocol to purpose?
exp: The four signature purposes - option A alone aligns them.

mcqs.q: Order the full access-decision pipeline:
exp: Claim identity, prove it (AuthN), get rights (AuthZ), leave records (accounting) - the AAA pipeline.
